en.title: Computer Science: the whole course
en.short: What a Computer Science degree covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Computer science is the study of computation: what can be computed, how to compute it efficiently, and how to build reliable systems that do it. It is not only programming. Programming is the main tool, in the same way that a laboratory is a tool for a chemist. The field also includes mathematics, engineering and the study of how people use technology.

The ideas last longer than the tools. Languages and frameworks change every few years. Binary search, relational algebra, the limits of computation and the principles of secure design change very little. A good degree teaches both, but it gives most weight to the lasting ideas.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
A first degree usually takes three or four years. In Nigeria, a BSc normally runs for four years, from 100 level to 400 level. The National Universities Commission (NUC) sets the minimum standards. Its older Benchmark Minimum Academic Standards (BMAS) are being replaced by the Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS), so check which set applies to your intake. Nigerian students also complete industrial training under SIWES. The Computing CCMAS asks for at least 24 weeks, with 12 weeks in each of the long vacations of 200 level and 300 level. Check your department’s handbook for the arrangements that apply to you. Polytechnics award the ND and HND under NBTE standards, with a stronger practical focus.

Degrees in Ghana and Kenya often take four years. In England, a degree usually takes three years, and in South Africa a three-year BSc may be followed by an Honours year. International curriculum guidance from ACM and the IEEE Computer Society influences many programmes. Most degrees end with an individual project. A master’s degree adds advanced courses and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The first year often builds foundations: programming, data representation, logic, sets and counting, basic data structures, and a first look at algorithm analysis and sorting.

The middle years build the core. In algorithms, you study trees, hash tables, graphs and design techniques. In systems, you study computer organisation, operating systems, databases and networks. Software engineering teaches you to build large programs in teams.

Later courses cover theory and specialist systems: automata, computability, complexity, compilers, security, web and mobile systems, and human-computer interaction.

At master’s level, common subjects include machine learning, distributed systems and research methods. Many programmes also offer options such as data science, robotics or computer vision.

The order varies. In Nigeria’s Computing CCMAS, programming and discrete structures come at 200 level, data structures and artificial intelligence at 300 level, and algorithms and research methodology at 400 level. The CCMAS sets 70% of the requirements as core, and each university adds the rest, so the core list does not name every topic here, such as compilers or automata.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Write code every week. You cannot learn programming only by reading. Type the examples, change them, and predict the result before you run them.

Trace algorithms by hand on small inputs. Many exam questions ask for the state of a structure after each step. Practise proofs in discrete mathematics and theory courses by writing every step in full. For complexity, practise counting operations until the method feels natural.

Build small complete projects, such as a results system for a department or a shop inventory. They connect databases, networks and user interfaces, and they give you work to show employers. Read error messages carefully. Use version control from the first year. If you use AI tools, follow your university’s rules, and make sure that you can explain every line that you submit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often make these mistakes:
Memorising code instead of understanding why it works.
Confusing best-case, average-case and worst-case complexity, or treating big O as an exact running time.
Forgetting edge cases, such as an empty list, a single item or the last index.
Saying that NP means “not polynomial”. It means “nondeterministic polynomial time”.
Treating a compiled program that runs as a correct program. It may still have logic errors.
Confusing similar terms: authentication and authorisation, process and thread, compiler and interpreter, TCP and UDP.
Learning one language or framework and neglecting the principles behind it.
Starting the final project late. Plan for time to test it and to write the report.

keyPoints: Computer science studies computation; programming is its main tool, not the whole subject.
Foundations come first, then algorithms and systems, then theory and specialist courses.
Standards differ by country, so check your own university’s current regulations.
Trace algorithms by hand and write code every week.
Principles last longer than any particular language or tool.

en.title: Programming fundamentals: variables, types and control flow
en.short: How programs store data and make decisions, how to trace them, and the main kinds of bug.

sections.heading: From source code to execution
sections.text:
A program is a precise set of instructions. A programmer writes it as source code in a high-level language. A compiler translates the whole program into a lower-level form before it runs. An interpreter executes the program step by step.

A variable is a named place that holds a value. A data type says what values are allowed and what operations make sense. Common types are integers, floating-point numbers, Booleans (true or false) and strings (text). Types matter. In many languages, 7 / 2 with two integers gives 3, while 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5. Check how your language treats this.

sections.heading: The three control structures
sections.text: Any algorithm can be written using three structures. Sequence means one step after another. Selection means choosing between steps with if and else. Iteration means repeating steps with a loop. A while loop repeats while a condition stays true. A for loop usually repeats over a range or a collection.

sections.heading: Worked example: tracing a loop
sections.text:
This pseudocode finds the mean of a list:
function average(numbers)
  total = 0
  for each x in numbers
    total = total + x
  return total / length(numbers)

Trace it with the list [4, 7, 10].
Start: total = 0
After x = 4: total = 4
After x = 7: total = 11
After x = 10: total = 21
Result: 21 / 3 = 7

Now ask what happens with an empty list. The function divides by zero. A careful programmer checks this case first.

sections.heading: Three kinds of bug
sections.text: A syntax error breaks the rules of the language, so the program does not compile or start. A runtime error stops the program during execution, for example a division by zero. A logic error is the most difficult, because the program runs but gives the wrong answer. A common logic error is the off-by-one error, where a loop runs one time too many or too few. Tracing by hand and testing edge cases find many of these errors.

keyPoints: A data type sets the allowed values and operations.
Sequence, selection and iteration are the three control structures.
Syntax, runtime and logic errors are different problems.
Trace code by hand with small inputs, including empty input.
Integer division can differ from floating-point division.

en.title: Functions, scope and recursion
en.short: How functions organise code, how the call stack works, and how to write correct recursion.

sections.heading: Why functions matter
sections.text:
A function is a named block of code that performs one task. It receives inputs called parameters and may return a result. Functions avoid repetition, and they let you think about a task without thinking about its details.

Scope is the part of a program where a name is valid. A variable declared inside a function is usually local, so other functions cannot see it. Languages also differ in how they pass arguments. With pass by value, the function receives a copy. With pass by reference, the function can change the caller’s variable. Many languages copy a reference to an object, so a function can change the object’s contents.

sections.heading: The call stack
sections.text: When a function is called, the system creates a stack frame. The frame holds the parameters, the local variables and the return address. When the function returns, its frame is removed.

sections.heading: Recursion and a worked example
sections.text:
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. It needs a base case, which stops the recursion, and a recursive case, which moves towards the base case.
function factorial(n)
  if n ≤ 1
    return 1
  return n * factorial(n - 1)

Trace factorial(4):
factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3)
factorial(3) = 3 × factorial(2)
factorial(2) = 2 × factorial(1)
factorial(1) = 1, the base case
Now the calls return: 2 × 1 = 2, then 3 × 2 = 6, then 4 × 6 = 24.

Each call waits for the next, so this function uses memory in proportion to n on the stack. With no base case, or with very deep recursion, the stack runs out of space. This failure is called a stack overflow.

sections.heading: Recursion or iteration?
sections.text: Every recursive function can be rewritten with a loop and, if necessary, an explicit stack. Recursion is often clearer for trees and for divide-and-conquer algorithms. It can also be wasteful. The simple recursive Fibonacci function repeats the same calls and takes exponential time, while a loop takes time proportional to n.

keyPoints: A function should do one clear task.
Each call creates a stack frame with its parameters and local variables.
Recursion needs a base case and progress towards it.
Too many nested calls cause a stack overflow.
Simple recursive Fibonacci takes exponential time; a loop takes linear time.

en.title: Object-oriented programming
en.short: Classes and objects, with encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction explained.

sections.heading: Classes and objects
sections.text:
Object-oriented programming organises a program around objects. An object combines data, called attributes or fields, with operations, called methods. A class is the description from which objects are made. Many objects can come from one class, and each has its own data.

This class describes a savings account in general pseudocode:
class Account
  private balance = 0
  method deposit(amount)
    if amount > 0
      balance = balance + amount
  method getBalance()
    return balance

If Ngozi’s account receives deposit(500) and then deposit(-100), the balance is 500. The method refuses the negative amount.

sections.heading: The four main principles
sections.text:
Encapsulation keeps data and its operations together and hides the data. In the example, other code cannot change balance directly. It must use deposit, so the rule about positive amounts always applies.

Abstraction means showing what an object does and hiding how it does it. A user of a list needs to know how to add an item, but not how the memory is arranged.

Inheritance lets a new class, the subclass, take on the attributes and methods of an existing class, the superclass. A SavingsAccount can inherit from Account and add interest. Inheritance should describe an “is a” relationship.

Polymorphism means that one call can behave differently depending on the object. Suppose that Rectangle and Circle both have an area method. A program can call area on every shape in a list. A rectangle of 3 by 4 returns 12, and a circle of radius 1 returns about 3.14. The calling code does not need to know each shape’s type.

sections.heading: Composition and interfaces
sections.text: Inheritance links classes tightly, so a change in a superclass can break its subclasses. Many designers therefore prefer composition where it fits. In composition, one object contains another, which describes a “has a” relationship: a Car has an Engine. An interface lists methods without giving their code, so different classes can provide them. Details differ between languages, but these ideas apply widely.

keyPoints: A class is a description; an object is an instance of it.
Encapsulation protects data by controlling access to it.
Inheritance means “is a”; composition means “has a”.
Polymorphism lets one call work with objects of different classes.
Abstraction hides how an operation is done.

en.title: Data representation: binary, integers, floats and text
en.short: How computers store numbers and text in bits, including two’s complement and floating point.

sections.heading: Bits, bytes and number bases
sections.text:
A bit holds 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, so it has 2⁸ = 256 possible patterns. In binary, each place is worth a power of 2. So 1101 = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.

Hexadecimal uses base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, which makes long binary values easier to read. For example, 0010 1101 = 2D in hex = 45 in decimal.

Size prefixes can cause confusion. A kilobyte (kB) is 1,000 bytes, while a kibibyte (KiB) is 1,024 bytes.

sections.heading: Signed integers: two’s complement
sections.text:
Most computers store signed integers in two’s complement. To negate a number, invert every bit and add 1.

Worked example: −13 in 8 bits.
13 = 00001101
Invert: 11110010
Add 1: 11110011, which is F3 in hex

With 8 bits, the range is −128 to 127. Overflow occurs when a result falls outside the range. In 8 bits, 127 + 1 wraps around to −128 on typical hardware.

sections.heading: Floating point
sections.text:
The IEEE 754 standard stores a real number as a sign, an exponent and a fraction. Single precision uses 32 bits: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. The exponent has a bias of 127.

Worked example: −6.25.
6.25 = 110.01 in binary = 1.1001 × 2²
Sign: 1
Exponent: 2 + 127 = 129 = 10000001
Fraction: 10010000000000000000000

Many decimal fractions have no exact binary form. So 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in double precision. Do not compare floats with == without care, and do not store money in floats. Use integer units or a decimal type.

sections.heading: Text
sections.text: A character set gives each character a number. ASCII covers 128 characters, and A is 65. Unicode covers the writing systems of the world. UTF-8 stores Unicode in 1 to 4 bytes, so A takes one byte and the naira sign ₦ takes three.

keyPoints: One hex digit equals 4 bits.
To negate in two’s complement, invert the bits and add 1.
An n-bit signed integer ranges from −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1.
Floating-point values are often approximate.
UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes for each Unicode character.

en.title: Logic and proof
en.short: Propositional and predicate logic, with direct proof, proof by contradiction and induction.

sections.heading: Propositional logic
sections.text:
A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. The main connectives are NOT (¬), AND (∧), OR (∨) and implication (→). The statement p → q is false in only one case: when p is true and q is false. It is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q.

The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p, and it has the same truth value. The converse, q → p, does not. De Morgan’s laws show how NOT acts on a compound statement:
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q

sections.heading: Predicate logic
sections.text: A predicate is a statement with variables, such as P(x): “x is even”. The universal quantifier ∀ means “for all”, and the existential quantifier ∃ means “there exists”. Negation swaps them. So ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). To disprove a claim about all values, one counterexample is enough.

sections.heading: Methods of proof
sections.text:
A direct proof starts from what is given and reaches the conclusion.
Claim: if n is even, then n² is even.
Proof: let n = 2k. Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is even.

Proof by contradiction assumes that the claim is false and then derives something impossible.

sections.heading: Mathematical induction
sections.text:
Induction proves a statement for all natural numbers. First prove a base case. Then assume that the statement holds for k, and prove that it holds for k + 1.

Claim: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 for all n ≥ 1.
Base case: for n = 1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1(2)/2 = 1.
Inductive step: assume that the formula holds for k. Then
1 + 2 + … + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1)
= (k + 1)(k + 2)/2
This is the formula with k + 1 in place of k. The proof is complete.

keyPoints: p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.
A statement and its contrapositive are equivalent; its converse is not.
Negation swaps ∀ and ∃.
One counterexample disproves a “for all” claim.
Induction needs a base case and an inductive step.

en.title: Sets, relations, functions and counting
en.short: The discrete mathematics behind databases and algorithms: sets, relations, functions and counting.

sections.heading: Sets
sections.text:
A set is a collection of distinct items. The main operations are union (A ∪ B), intersection (A ∩ B), difference (A − B) and complement. The power set of A is the set of all its subsets. If A has n elements, its power set has 2ⁿ.

Inclusion-exclusion counts a union: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
Worked example: in a class of 120, 70 students take Statistics, 50 take Physics and 30 take both. Then 70 + 50 − 30 = 90 take at least one.

sections.heading: Relations and functions
sections.text:
A relation on a set A is a set of ordered pairs from A. It may be reflexive (every a relates to itself), symmetric (if a relates to b, then b relates to a) or transitive (if a relates to b and b to c, then a relates to c). A relation with all three properties is an equivalence relation.

A function assigns exactly one output to each input. It is injective if different inputs give different outputs. It is surjective if every possible output is reached. It is bijective if it is both.

sections.heading: Counting
sections.text:
The product rule says that independent choices multiply. A code of three letters and two digits has 26³ × 10² = 1,757,600 possibilities, if repeats are allowed.

Permutations count ordered selections, and combinations count unordered ones. Choosing 2 of 5 people:
For a chair and a secretary: P(5, 2) = 5!/3! = 20
For a committee of two: C(5, 2) = 5!/(2! 3!) = 10

The pigeonhole principle says that if n + 1 items go into n boxes, one box holds at least two items. It explains why a hash table with more keys than slots must have collisions.

sections.heading: Modular arithmetic
sections.text: The expression a mod m gives the remainder when a is divided by m. So 17 mod 5 = 2.

keyPoints: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
A bijection is both injective and surjective.
Order matters in permutations but not in combinations.
The pigeonhole principle explains why collisions cannot always be avoided.

en.title: Probability and statistics for computing
en.short: Conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, common distributions and how to summarise measured data.

sections.heading: Probability and Bayes’ rule
sections.text:
Probability describes uncertain events. A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes, and an event is a set of outcomes.

The probability of A given B is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Events A and B are independent when P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional probability:
P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) ÷ P(B)

Worked example: 1% of transactions are fraud. A detector flags 90% of fraud and 5% of genuine transactions.
P(flag) = 0.01 × 0.9 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0585
P(fraud | flag) = 0.009 ÷ 0.0585 ≈ 0.15
Only about 15% of flags are real fraud, because genuine transactions are so common.

sections.heading: Random variables and distributions
sections.text:
A random variable gives a number to each outcome. Its expected value is the long-run average, and its variance measures the spread around that average.

Binomial: successes in n independent trials with the same probability p. The mean is np.
Geometric: trials up to and including the first success. The mean is 1/p. Some books count only the failures.
Poisson: events in a fixed interval, when they occur independently at a steady rate.
Normal: the continuous bell curve, set by its mean and standard deviation.

Worked example: a link loses each packet independently with probability 0.1. Out of 10 packets, the expected number lost is 10 × 0.1 = 1. The probability of losing none is 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Worked example: five response times are 4, 7, 7, 10 and 22 ms.
Mean = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 ms
Median = 7 ms
Sample variance = (36 + 9 + 9 + 0 + 144) ÷ 4 = 49.5
Standard deviation ≈ 7.0 ms

One slow response pulls the mean above the median, so report both. The central limit theorem says that, under broad conditions, the mean of a large sample is approximately normal.

keyPoints: Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional probability.
When an event is rare, most alarms can be false even with a good detector.
Independent events satisfy P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
A binomial variable has mean np; a geometric variable has mean 1/p.
An outlier moves the mean more than the median.
A sample variance divides by n − 1.

en.title: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues
en.short: The basic linear data structures, what each operation costs, and when to use each one.

sections.heading: Arrays and linked lists
sections.text:
A data structure is a way of arranging data so that certain operations are efficient. An array stores items in adjacent memory locations. Because the address of any item can be calculated from its index, access by index takes O(1) time. Inserting in the middle takes O(n), because later items must move.

A dynamic array grows by allocating a larger block and copying the items. It usually doubles its capacity. A single append may take O(n) time, but the average over many appends is O(1). This average is called the amortised cost.

A linked list stores each item in a node, with a reference to the next node. Inserting at the head takes O(1). Reaching the item at position i takes O(i), because you must follow the links. Arrays are often faster in practice.

sections.heading: Stacks and queues
sections.text: A stack is last in, first out (LIFO). Its main operations are push and pop. It supports function calls, undo features and expression evaluation. A queue is first in, first out (FIFO). Its main operations are enqueue and dequeue. It suits print jobs, breadth-first search and customers waiting for service. Good implementations of both perform these operations in O(1) time.

sections.heading: Worked example: balanced brackets
sections.text:
A stack can check whether brackets match, which is one of the tasks a compiler performs:
function isBalanced(text)
  stack = empty list
  for each ch in text
    if ch == "("
      append(stack, ch)
    else if ch == ")"
      if length(stack) == 0
        return false
      removeLast(stack)
  return length(stack) == 0

For "(a(b)c)", the stack grows to two items and returns to empty, so the result is true.
For "(()", one item remains, so the result is false.
For ")(", the first character finds an empty stack, so the result is false. A simple count of each bracket type would miss this case, because the counts are equal.

The function makes one pass and uses O(n) time. In the worst case, it uses O(n) memory.

keyPoints: Array access by index is O(1); middle insertion is O(n).
Dynamic array append is amortised O(1).
Linked lists need O(i) time to reach position i.
A stack is LIFO; a queue is FIFO.
The choice of structure depends on which operations are most frequent.

en.title: Algorithm analysis and big O notation
en.short: How to measure the growth of running time and memory, using big O, big Omega and big Theta.

sections.heading: Why count operations
sections.text:
To compare algorithms in general, we count basic operations as a function of the input size n. We focus on how the count grows as n becomes large.

We usually study the worst case, because it gives a guarantee.

sections.heading: The notation
sections.text:
f(n) = O(g(n)) means that there are positive constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. This is an upper bound on growth. Big Omega (Ω) gives a lower bound, and big Theta (Θ) gives both, so it is a tight bound.

Worked example: show that 3n² + 5n + 2 = O(n²).
For n ≥ 1, 5n ≤ 5n² and 2 ≤ 2n².
So 3n² + 5n + 2 ≤ 3n² + 5n² + 2n² = 10n².
Take c = 10 and n₀ = 1.

Big O is not limited to the worst case. Each case has its own bound, so insertion sort takes Θ(n) in its best case and Θ(n²) in its worst.

sections.heading: Counting loops
sections.text:
This function counts pairs of equal items:
function countPairs(a)
  count = 0
  n = length(a)
  for i = 0 to n - 2
    for j = i + 1 to n - 1
      if a[i] == a[j]
        count = count + 1
  return count

For n items, the inner test runs (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 times, which is Θ(n²). With n = 5, it runs 10 times.

Halving the problem gives logarithmic growth. A value of one million can be halved only about 20 times before it reaches 1.

sections.heading: What growth means in practice
sections.text:
The common orders, from slow growth to fast, are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ) and O(n!).

Consider n = 1,000,000 on a machine doing 10⁹ simple operations each second. An O(n log n) method needs about 2 × 10⁷ operations, or 0.02 seconds. An O(n²) method needs 10¹² operations, or about 17 minutes.

keyPoints: Big O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound and Θ a tight bound.
Drop constants and lower-order terms when stating growth.
Nested loops over n items often give Θ(n²).
Repeated halving gives logarithmic growth.
Space complexity measures memory use in the same way.

en.title: Searching and sorting
en.short: Linear and binary search, then the main sorting algorithms with their costs and properties.

sections.heading: Searching
sections.text:
Linear search checks each item in turn and takes O(n) time. Binary search needs a sorted array. It compares the target with the middle item and discards half of the range, so it takes O(log n) time.
function binarySearch(a, target)
  low = 0
  high = length(a) - 1
  while low ≤ high
    mid = floor((low + high) / 2)
    if a[mid] == target
      return mid
    else if a[mid] < target
      low = mid + 1
    else
      high = mid - 1
  return -1

Worked example: search for 57 in [3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 57, 61, 75].
mid = 3, a[3] = 23, too small, so low = 4
mid = 5, a[5] = 57, found at index 5

sections.heading: Simple sorting
sections.text:
Insertion sort takes each item and moves it left into position among the items already sorted.

It takes Θ(n²) time in the worst case but Θ(n) on a list that is already sorted. It is stable, it works in place, and it is fast on short lists.

sections.heading: Efficient sorting
sections.text:
Merge sort divides the list in half, sorts each half, and merges the results. Its time is Θ(n log n) in every case. It is stable, but the usual array version needs O(n) extra memory.

Quicksort chooses a pivot, moves smaller items to one side and larger items to the other, and then sorts each side. Its average time is O(n log n) and its worst case is O(n²). It is usually not stable, but it is often fast in practice.

Heapsort uses a heap, takes O(n log n) time in the worst case and works in place. It is not stable.

A sort is stable if equal items keep their original order.

sections.heading: The lower bound
sections.text: Any sort that works only by comparing items needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Counting sort does not compare items. It takes O(n + k) time when the keys are integers in a range of size k.

keyPoints: Binary search needs sorted data and takes O(log n) time.
Merge sort is Θ(n log n) in all cases and is stable.
Quicksort averages O(n log n) but has an O(n²) worst case.
Comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
Counting sort takes O(n + k) on small integer keys.

en.title: Trees, heaps and hash tables
en.short: Binary search trees, balanced trees, heaps and hash tables, with their costs and common uses.

sections.heading: Binary search trees
sections.text:
A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges, with one root and no cycles. In a binary search tree (BST), each node has at most two children. Keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node’s key, and keys in the right subtree are larger.

Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 in that order. The root is 50, its children are 30 and 70, and 30 has the children 20 and 40. An in-order traversal visits left, node, right, so it gives the sorted order: 20, 30, 40, 50, 70.

Search and insertion take time proportional to the height. Sorted input produces a tree shaped like a list, with O(n) height. Balanced trees, such as AVL and red-black trees, rotate nodes to keep the height at O(log n). B-trees have many children at each node, which reduces disk reads, so databases use them for indexes.

sections.heading: Heaps
sections.text: A binary min-heap is a complete tree in which each parent is no larger than its children. The smallest item is therefore at the root. In an array, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Reading the minimum takes O(1), and insertion and removal take O(log n). A heap is the usual way to implement a priority queue.

sections.heading: Hash tables
sections.text:
A hash table uses a hash function to turn a key into an array index. Lookup, insertion and deletion take O(1) on average. Their worst case is O(n).

A collision occurs when two keys get the same index. Chaining keeps a list at each index. Open addressing looks for another free slot.

Worked example: use h(k) = k mod 7 with the keys 15, 22, 8 and 10. The indexes are 1, 1, 1 and 3, so three keys collide at index 1. The load factor is keys ÷ slots = 4/7, or about 0.57.

keyPoints: BST operations take time proportional to the tree’s height.
Balanced trees guarantee O(log n) height.
An in-order traversal of a BST gives sorted keys.
A heap supports a priority queue with O(log n) updates.
Hash tables are O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case.

en.title: Graphs and graph algorithms
en.short: Graph representations, BFS and DFS, shortest paths, spanning trees and topological sorting.

sections.heading: Representing graphs
sections.text:
A graph has vertices joined by edges. Edges may be directed and may have weights. V is the number of vertices, and E is the number of edges.

An adjacency matrix uses O(V²) memory and tests for an edge in O(1). An adjacency list uses O(V + E) memory and is better for sparse graphs.

sections.heading: Traversal
sections.text:
Breadth-first search (BFS) visits vertices level by level with a queue. In an unweighted graph, it finds the shortest path by number of edges.

Consider undirected edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D and D-E. From A, the distances are B = 1, C = 1, D = 2 and E = 3.

Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible and then backtracks, using recursion or a stack. Both BFS and DFS take O(V + E) time with adjacency lists. A topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that each edge goes forward.

sections.heading: Shortest paths: Dijkstra
sections.text:
Dijkstra’s algorithm repeatedly takes the closest unfinished vertex and relaxes its outgoing edges. To relax an edge means to check whether going through it gives a shorter path. The algorithm needs non-negative weights. With a binary heap, it takes O((V + E) log V) time. Bellman-Ford allows negative weights and detects negative cycles, but it takes O(VE) time.

Worked example with directed edges: A→B 4, A→C 1, C→B 2, C→D 8, B→D 5.
Start from A: A = 0, B = 4, C = 1.
Finish C: B falls to 1 + 2 = 3, and D = 1 + 8 = 9.
Finish B: D falls to 3 + 5 = 8.
Result: A = 0, C = 1, B = 3, D = 8.

sections.heading: Minimum spanning trees
sections.text: A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a connected, weighted, undirected graph at the lowest total weight. Kruskal’s algorithm adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. Prim’s algorithm grows one tree outward from a starting vertex.

keyPoints: Adjacency lists use O(V + E) memory; matrices use O(V²).
BFS uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS uses a stack or recursion.
Dijkstra needs non-negative edge weights.
Kruskal and Prim find minimum spanning trees.

en.title: Algorithm design: divide and conquer, greedy and dynamic programming
en.short: The main strategies for designing algorithms, how to choose one, and the master theorem.

sections.heading: Divide and conquer
sections.text:
Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller parts, solves each part recursively and combines the results. Its running time is written as a recurrence. Merge sort has T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n).

The master theorem solves many recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a). For merge sort, a = 2 and b = 2, so n^(log_b a) = n. This matches f(n), which gives T(n) = Θ(n log n).

sections.heading: Greedy algorithms
sections.text: A greedy algorithm makes the choice that looks best now and never reconsiders it. It is often simple and fast, but it is correct only for some problems, so it needs a proof. For example, if you want to attend the most non-overlapping activities, repeatedly choosing the activity that finishes first gives an optimal result.

sections.heading: Dynamic programming
sections.text:
Dynamic programming (DP) applies when a problem has two properties. Optimal substructure means that an optimal answer is built from optimal answers to smaller problems. Overlapping subproblems means that the same smaller problems occur many times. DP stores each answer so that it is computed only once. Top-down DP with stored answers is called memoisation. Bottom-up DP fills a table.

Worked example: make an amount using the fewest coins, with values 1, 3 and 4 and a total of 6.
function minCoins(coins, amount)
  best = filled(amount + 1, infinity)
  best[0] = 0
  for a = 1 to amount
    for each c in coins
      if c ≤ a and best[a - c] + 1 < best[a]
        best[a] = best[a - c] + 1
  return best[amount]

The table of best values for amounts 0 to 6 is 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2. So the answer is 2, using 3 + 3. A greedy method takes 4 first and then 1 + 1, which uses 3 coins. The time is O(amount × number of coins).

keyPoints: Divide and conquer: split, solve recursively, combine.
A greedy algorithm needs a proof that it is correct.
DP needs optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
Memoisation is top-down; a table is bottom-up.
Merge sort’s recurrence solves to Θ(n log n).

en.title: Digital logic and computer organisation
en.short: Logic gates, the CPU, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, instruction sets and assembly language.

sections.heading: From gates to circuits
sections.text:
Logic gates such as AND, OR, NOT and XOR compute Boolean functions on bits. Gates combine into larger circuits.

A half adder adds two bits, A and B:
Sum = A XOR B
Carry = A AND B
With A = 1 and B = 1, Sum = 0 and Carry = 1, which is binary 10, or 2.

A full adder also accepts a carry from the previous column, and a chain of full adders adds whole numbers. Combinational circuits give outputs that depend only on the current inputs. Sequential circuits, such as flip-flops and registers, also store state.

sections.heading: Inside the processor
sections.text:
Most computers follow the von Neumann design, in which instructions and data share one memory. The central processing unit (CPU) contains the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), which performs calculations, and the control unit, which directs each step. It also contains registers, which are small and very fast storage locations. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, and the instruction register holds the current one.

Each instruction passes through a cycle:
Fetch: read the instruction from memory, then advance the program counter.
Decode: work out the operation and the operands.
Execute: perform the operation, then store the result.

sections.heading: Instruction sets
sections.text:
The instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and hardware. It defines the instructions, registers and addressing modes. RISC designs use fewer, simpler and more regular instructions. CISC designs include more complex instructions. The boundary is less sharp than it once was, because modern CISC processors usually break instructions into simpler internal steps.

Assembly language is a readable form of machine code. This sketch uses an invented simple machine with one accumulator register:
LOAD 100
ADD 101
STORE 102
The accumulator receives the value at address 100, then adds the value at address 101. Finally, the sum goes to address 102. If those addresses held 7 and 5, address 102 now holds 12.

keyPoints: A half adder gives Sum = A XOR B and Carry = A AND B.
The CPU repeats fetch, decode and execute.
The program counter holds the next instruction’s address.
The ISA is the interface between software and hardware.
Sequential circuits store state; combinational circuits do not.

en.title: Memory hierarchy, pipelining and performance
en.short: Caches, locality, pipelining and hazards, the CPU time formula and Amdahl’s law.

sections.heading: The memory hierarchy
sections.text:
Fast memory is expensive and small, while large memory is cheaper and slow. Computers therefore use a hierarchy: registers, then cache levels, then main memory, then solid-state or magnetic storage.

This design works because of locality. Temporal locality means that a recently used item is likely to be used again soon. Spatial locality means that nearby items are likely to be used soon. Programs that walk through an array in order therefore tend to run well.

A cache stores blocks of memory.

Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
Worked example: with a hit time of 1 ns, a miss rate of 5% and a miss penalty of 100 ns, the average is 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 ns.

sections.heading: Pipelining
sections.text:
A pipeline divides each instruction into stages, such as fetch, decode, execute, memory access and write back. Several instructions can then be in progress at once. Pipelining improves throughput, but it does not shorten the time of a single instruction.

Hazards interrupt the flow. A structural hazard occurs when two instructions need the same hardware. A data hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result that is not ready yet. Forwarding reduces its cost. A control hazard comes from branches, and branch prediction reduces its cost.

sections.heading: Measuring performance
sections.text:
CPU time = instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) ÷ clock rate.
Worked example: 2 × 10⁹ instructions at a CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz processor take (2 × 10⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3 × 10⁹) = 1 second.

Amdahl’s law limits the gain from parallel hardware. If a fraction p of the work can run in parallel on n processors, the speedup is 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p/n). With p = 0.9 and n = 10, the speedup is 1 ÷ (0.1 + 0.09), or about 5.26. Even with unlimited processors, it cannot exceed 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10.

keyPoints: Caches work because of temporal and spatial locality.
Average access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of one instruction.
Hazards are structural, data or control.
Amdahl’s law: the serial part limits the total speedup.

en.title: Operating systems: processes, scheduling and concurrency
en.short: Processes and threads, CPU scheduling, race conditions, locks and the conditions for deadlock.

sections.heading: Processes and threads
sections.text: An operating system (OS) manages hardware and provides services to programs. A process is a program in execution, with its own address space. A thread is a path of execution within a process. Threads in one process share memory.

sections.heading: Scheduling
sections.text:
The scheduler chooses which ready process runs next. Waiting time is the time a process spends ready but not running.

Worked example: three processes arrive at time 0, with bursts of P1 = 5, P2 = 3 and P3 = 1.
First come, first served, in the order P1, P2, P3: waits are 0, 5 and 8. The mean is 13/3, or about 4.33.
Shortest job first, in the order P3, P2, P1: waits are 0, 1 and 4. The mean is 5/3, or about 1.67.
Round robin with a time slice of 2 runs P1, P2, P3, P1, P2, P1. The finish times are P3 = 5, P2 = 8 and P1 = 9. The waits are P1 = 4, P2 = 5 and P3 = 4, with a mean of about 4.33.

Shortest job first gives the lowest mean wait for jobs that arrive together, but it needs burst lengths in advance, and long jobs can starve.

sections.heading: Race conditions and synchronisation
sections.text:
A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of threads. Suppose that two threads both add 1 to a shared counter holding 10. Each reads 10, each computes 11, and each writes 11. One update is lost.

The code that uses shared data is a critical section. A mutex lock allows one thread at a time to enter it. A semaphore is a counter with atomic wait and signal operations, and it can limit access to several units of a resource.

sections.heading: Deadlock
sections.text: A deadlock occurs when threads wait for each other forever. It requires four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Removing any one condition prevents it.

keyPoints: A process has its own address space; threads share one.
Shortest job first minimises the mean wait but can starve long jobs.
A race condition depends on timing, and it can lose updates.
A mutex protects a critical section.
Deadlock needs all four conditions at once.

en.title: Operating systems: memory management and file systems
en.short: Virtual memory, paging, address translation, page replacement and how file systems store data.

sections.heading: Virtual memory and paging
sections.text:
Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, which protects processes from each other. It also allows programs to use more memory than is physically present, by keeping some data on storage.

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size. A page table maps pages to frames. Because this lookup takes time, processors keep recent translations in a small cache called the translation lookaside buffer (TLB).

Worked example: the page size is 4 KiB, or 4,096 bytes, and the virtual address is 20,500.
Page number = floor(20,500 ÷ 4,096) = 5
Offset = 20,500 − 5 × 4,096 = 20
If the page table maps page 5 to frame 2, the physical address is 2 × 4,096 + 20 = 8,212.

sections.heading: Page replacement
sections.text:
A page fault occurs when a program uses a page that is not in memory. The OS loads it and may remove another page.

Worked example: three frames and the references 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2.
FIFO removes the oldest loaded page. The references to 1, 2 and 3 fault. The next 1 is a hit. Then 4 removes 1, 1 removes 2, and 2 removes 3. That gives 6 faults.
LRU removes the least recently used page. The references to 1, 2 and 3 fault, and the next 1 is a hit. Then 4 removes 2, the following 1 is a hit, and 2 removes 3. That gives 5 faults.

Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time moving pages than doing useful work.

sections.heading: File systems
sections.text:
A file system organises data on storage into files and directories. It records metadata such as size, owner, permissions and the location of the data. Unix-like systems keep it in an inode.

A journaling file system first records the intended changes in a log, so it can recover quickly after a crash. It does not replace backups.

keyPoints: Paging maps virtual pages to physical frames of the same size.
Page number = address ÷ page size; the offset is the remainder.
The TLB caches recent address translations.
LRU is usually better than FIFO, but not on every input.
Journaling helps recovery, but it does not replace backups.

en.title: Relational databases and SQL
en.short: The relational model, keys, entity-relationship design, relational algebra, SQL and indexes.

sections.heading: The relational model
sections.text:
A database management system (DBMS) stores data and controls access to it. The relational model holds data in tables, also called relations. A row is a tuple, and a column is an attribute.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row. A foreign key refers to a primary key in another table, which links the tables and protects referential integrity. An entity-relationship (ER) diagram is often the first step in design. It shows entities, their attributes and their relationships. A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, needs a separate linking table.

Relational algebra gives the theory behind queries. Selection chooses rows, projection chooses columns, and join combines tables on matching values.

sections.heading: Worked example in SQL
sections.text:
Consider two tables:
student(id, name)
enrolment(student_id, course_code, score)

The data are:
Amina (id 1): scores 70 and 80
Kwame (id 2): scores 50 and 58
Thabo (id 3): score 65

This query lists students whose mean score is at least 60, highest first:
SELECT s.name, AVG(e.score) AS mean_score
FROM student s
JOIN enrolment e ON e.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
HAVING AVG(e.score) >= 60
ORDER BY mean_score DESC;

The result is Amina 75, then Thabo 65. Kwame’s mean of 54 is excluded. WHERE filters rows before grouping, while HAVING filters groups after it.

An inner join keeps only matching rows. A left join keeps every row of the left table and fills missing values with NULL. Comparisons with NULL give an unknown result, so write IS NULL, not = NULL.

sections.heading: Indexes
sections.text:
Without an index, the DBMS may scan a whole table. An index, usually a B-tree, lets it find rows in about O(log n) steps. Indexes speed up reads, but they use storage and slow down writes.

Non-relational systems, often called NoSQL, use documents, key-value pairs, wide columns or graphs. They suit some workloads, for example very large or changing data, but relational databases remain the usual choice for structured business data.

keyPoints: A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key links tables.
Many-to-many relationships need a linking table.
WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.
Use IS NULL to test for missing values.
Indexes speed up reads and slow down writes.

en.title: Normalisation and transactions
en.short: How to remove redundancy with normal forms, and how ACID transactions keep data correct.

sections.heading: Why normalise
sections.text:
Redundant data causes anomalies. An update anomaly occurs when a change must be repeated in many rows. An insertion anomaly occurs when you cannot record one fact without another. A deletion anomaly occurs when removing a row loses another fact.

A functional dependency X → Y means that the value of X determines the value of Y.

sections.heading: Worked example: the normal forms
sections.text:
Consider this table, with the key (StudentID, CourseCode):
Result(StudentID, StudentName, DeptCode, DeptName, CourseCode, CourseTitle, Score)

First normal form (1NF) requires atomic values, with no repeating groups. Assume that the table already meets this.

Second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key. StudentName depends on StudentID alone, and CourseTitle depends on CourseCode alone. So we split:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, DeptCode, DeptName)
Course(CourseCode, CourseTitle)
Result(StudentID, CourseCode, Score)

Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. StudentID determines DeptCode, and DeptCode determines DeptName. So we split again:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, DeptCode)
Department(DeptCode, DeptName)

Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is stricter: in every non-trivial dependency X → Y, X must be a superkey.

sections.heading: Transactions and ACID
sections.text:
A transaction is a group of operations that act as one unit. Think of moving ₦5,000 between two accounts: one debit and one credit must both happen.

Atomicity: all of the operations happen, or none do.
Consistency: the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another.
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere in unintended ways.
Durability: committed changes survive a crash. Write-ahead logging supports this, because changes are recorded in a log before they reach the data files.

sections.heading: Concurrency control
sections.text: Without control, two transactions can cause a lost update or read uncommitted data, which is called a dirty read. Two-phase locking first acquires locks, then releases them, and never acquires a lock after a release. This guarantees serialisable schedules, but deadlock remains possible. SQL defines isolation levels from read uncommitted to serialisable.

keyPoints: 2NF removes partial dependencies on a composite key.
3NF removes transitive dependencies.
ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
Write-ahead logging supports recovery and durability.
Two-phase locking ensures serialisability, but deadlock is possible.

en.title: Computer networks: layers and IP addressing
en.short: The OSI and TCP/IP models, encapsulation, switches and routers, subnetting and network delay.

sections.heading: Why networks use layers
sections.text:
A network divides its work into layers, and each layer uses the services of the layer below. The OSI reference model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. The TCP/IP model used on the internet has fewer. It is usually taught with four layers, or five when the physical and link layers are counted separately.

Encapsulation means that each layer adds its own header as data moves down. An application message goes into a transport segment, then an IP packet, then a link-layer frame. The receiver removes the headers in reverse order.

sections.heading: Devices and addresses
sections.text:
A switch works at the link layer and forwards frames using MAC addresses, which identify network interfaces on the local network. A router works at the network layer and forwards packets between networks using IP addresses. The MAC addresses change at each hop, while the source and destination IP addresses normally stay the same, unless NAT changes them.

IPv4 addresses have 32 bits, and IPv6 addresses have 128 bits. Network address translation (NAT) lets many devices with private addresses share a single public address.

sections.heading: Worked example: subnetting
sections.text:
CIDR notation shows how many bits identify the network. Consider 192.168.10.0/26.
Host bits: 32 − 26 = 6
Addresses in each subnet: 2⁶ = 64
Usable hosts: 64 − 2 = 62, because the first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address
Mask: 255.255.255.192
First subnet: 192.168.10.0 to 192.168.10.63

Which subnet holds 192.168.10.75? Subnets start at multiples of 64, so it is in the subnet 192.168.10.64/26, which ends at .127.

sections.heading: Delay
sections.text:
A packet’s total delay has four parts: processing, queueing, transmission and propagation. Transmission delay is the packet size divided by the link rate. Propagation delay is the distance divided by the signal speed.

A packet of 1,500 bytes on a 100 Mbit/s link has a transmission delay of (1,500 × 8) ÷ (100 × 10⁶) = 120 µs.

keyPoints: OSI has seven layers; the TCP/IP model has four or five.
Switches use MAC addresses; routers use IP addresses.
A /26 subnet has 64 addresses and 62 usable hosts.
Transmission delay is size ÷ rate.
Check whether a figure uses bits or bytes.

en.title: Computer networks: TCP, UDP, DNS and HTTP
en.short: How TCP gives reliable delivery, when to use UDP, and how DNS and HTTP work together.

sections.heading: TCP and UDP
sections.text:
The transport layer connects programs rather than machines. Port numbers identify the programs.

TCP is connection-oriented. A connection begins with a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. TCP numbers the bytes, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits what is lost and delivers data in order.

UDP has no connection and gives no guarantee of delivery or order. It adds little overhead, so it suits short queries and live media, where a late packet is no longer useful.

sections.heading: Flow and congestion control
sections.text:
Flow control protects the receiver. In TCP, the receiver advertises a window, which limits how much unacknowledged data the sender may have in transit. Congestion control protects the network. The sender reduces its rate when it detects signs of congestion, such as packet loss.

With a sliding window, the maximum throughput is about window size ÷ round-trip time.
Worked example: a window of 64,000 bytes and a round-trip time of 100 ms give 64,000 ÷ 0.1 = 640,000 bytes per second, which is 5.12 Mbit/s.

sections.heading: DNS, DHCP and HTTP
sections.text:
DHCP gives a device its IP address and other settings when it joins a network. The Domain Name System (DNS) translates names into IP addresses. It is a distributed hierarchy of root, top-level domain and authoritative servers.

HTTP is the application protocol of the web. A client sends a request, and the server sends a response. Every request is independent, so HTTP is called stateless. HTTPS runs HTTP over TLS, which encrypts the data and checks the server’s identity.

sections.heading: Example: opening a web page
sections.text:
Suppose that Fatima enters a web address on her phone.
1. The phone asks DNS for the server’s IP address, unless the answer is already cached.
2. The phone opens a connection to that address. With TCP, this starts with the handshake.
3. TLS sets up encryption.
4. The browser sends an HTTP GET request.
5. The server returns a response, for example with status 200, and the page.
6. The browser requests further files, such as images and scripts.

keyPoints: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is lightweight and gives no guarantee.
The TCP handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.
DNS maps names to IP addresses.
HTTP is stateless; HTTPS adds TLS.

en.title: Software engineering: process and requirements
en.short: Life-cycle models, agile working, requirements, version control and professional responsibility.

sections.heading: What software engineering is
sections.text:
Software engineering applies disciplined methods to building and maintaining software. A large system needs many people over many years, so communication, planning and maintenance become central problems.

The usual activities are requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Together, they form the software development life cycle (SDLC).

sections.heading: Process models
sections.text:
The waterfall model completes each activity before the next begins. It suits work with stable requirements and strict documentation, but late changes cost a lot.

Iterative models build the system in repeated cycles, so users can give feedback early. Agile methods extend this idea. They value short cycles, working software, close contact with users and readiness for change. In Scrum, a common agile framework, the team works in short periods called sprints, often of two to four weeks. It takes work from a prioritised list called the product backlog.

No model suits every project. A safety-critical system needs more formal evidence than a small mobile app.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text:
Requirements state what a system must do. Functional requirements describe behaviour. Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as speed, security and availability. Good requirements can be tested.

Example for a mobile payment system used in Kenya and Ghana:
Functional: a user can send money to another registered user.
Weak non-functional: transfers must be fast.
Better non-functional: 95% of transfers finish within 3 seconds at the expected peak load.

Find requirements by talking to stakeholders, observing their work and building prototypes.

sections.heading: Working as a team
sections.text:
Version control records every change and lets people work on the same code. Developers commonly work on separate branches and then merge their work after review. Continuous integration builds and tests each change automatically, so that problems appear early.

Engineers also have professional duties. They must protect users’ data, respect licences, tell the truth about risks and estimate honestly. Professional bodies such as ACM set out expectations. In Nigeria, the Computer Professionals (Registration Council of Nigeria), or CPN, is the statutory regulator of the profession.

keyPoints: The SDLC covers requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
Waterfall works in sequence; agile works in short cycles.
Functional requirements state behaviour; non-functional requirements state qualities.
A good requirement can be tested.
Version control and continuous integration catch problems early.

en.title: Software design and testing
en.short: Modularity, cohesion and coupling, UML, design patterns, testing levels and test case design.

sections.heading: Principles of design
sections.text: Good design makes a system easy to understand and change. Modularity divides a system into parts with clear interfaces. Aim for high cohesion, which means that each module has one focused purpose. Also aim for low coupling, which means that modules depend on each other as little as possible. Then a change in one module rarely forces changes in others.

sections.heading: UML and patterns
sections.text:
The Unified Modeling Language (UML) offers standard diagrams. A use case diagram shows how users interact with a system. A class diagram shows classes and their relationships. A sequence diagram shows the messages between objects over time.

A design pattern is a tested, reusable solution to a common design problem. For example, the observer pattern lets many objects receive updates from one object without being tightly coupled to it.

sections.heading: Levels of testing
sections.text:
Testing can show that faults exist, but it cannot prove that there are none.
Unit tests check small parts alone.
Integration tests check that parts work together.
System tests check the whole system against its requirements.
Acceptance tests check that it meets the needs of users.
Regression tests are repeated after changes, to confirm that working features still work.

sections.heading: Designing test cases
sections.text:
Black-box testing uses the specification. White-box testing uses the code’s structure.

Worked example: a loan form accepts ages from 18 to 65 inclusive. Equivalence partitioning divides inputs into groups that should behave alike: below 18, 18 to 65, and above 65. Choose one value from each group, such as 10, 40 and 70. Boundary value analysis tests the edges, where mistakes are common: 17, 18, 65 and 66.

Cyclomatic complexity measures the number of independent paths through code: V(G) = E − N + 2P. Here, E is the number of edges, N the number of nodes and P the number of connected parts in the control-flow graph. For a single function with only simple decisions, it equals the number of decisions + 1. So two if statements give 3.

keyPoints: Aim for high cohesion and low coupling.
Testing can reveal faults but cannot prove their absence.
Test levels: unit, integration, system and acceptance.
Boundary value analysis tests values at the edges of ranges.
Regression tests confirm that changes have not broken working features.

en.title: Theory of computation: automata and formal languages
en.short: Finite automata, regular expressions, context-free grammars and the Chomsky hierarchy.

sections.heading: Languages and finite automata
sections.text:
In this theory, an alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of symbols, and a language is a set of strings. An automaton is an abstract machine that decides whether a string belongs to a language.

A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) has a finite set of states, one start state, some accepting states and exactly one transition for each state and symbol.

Worked example: a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts strings with an even number of 0s has two states, Even and Odd. Even is both the start state and the accepting state. Reading 0 switches the state. Reading 1 keeps the state.
Input 1001: Even, Even, Odd, Even, Even. The machine accepts.

sections.heading: Regular languages
sections.text:
A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) may have several possible moves. It accepts if any path accepts. NFAs are no more powerful than DFAs, because the subset construction converts any NFA to a DFA.

Regular expressions describe exactly the same class of languages, called the regular languages. For example, (0|1)*1 describes binary strings that end in 1.

Some languages are not regular. The language {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} needs unlimited counting, which a finite number of states cannot do. The pumping lemma is the standard tool for proving this. It can show that a language is not regular, but it cannot show that a language is regular.

sections.heading: Context-free languages
sections.text:
A context-free grammar (CFG) has rules that replace a single variable. This grammar generates {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}:
S → 0S1 | ε
Here ε means the empty string.

A nondeterministic pushdown automaton, a finite automaton with a stack, recognises exactly the context-free languages. The deterministic version recognises fewer.

sections.heading: The Chomsky hierarchy
sections.text:
The hierarchy runs from least to most general:
Type 3: regular languages, recognised by finite automata
Type 2: context-free languages, recognised by pushdown automata
Type 1: context-sensitive languages, recognised by linear bounded automata
Type 0: recursively enumerable languages, recognised by Turing machines

keyPoints: DFAs and NFAs recognise the same languages.
Regular expressions describe exactly the regular languages.
{0ⁿ1ⁿ} is context-free but not regular.
A pushdown automaton adds a stack to a finite automaton.
The pumping lemma can only show that a language is not regular.

en.title: Theory of computation: computability and complexity
en.short: Turing machines, the halting problem, reductions, and the classes P, NP and NP-complete.

sections.heading: Turing machines and computability
sections.text:
A Turing machine has a finite control and an unlimited tape that it can read and write. It can carry out any algorithm that a modern computer can. The Church-Turing thesis states that anything computable by an effective procedure can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because “effective procedure” is an informal idea.

A language is decidable if some Turing machine always halts and gives the correct answer. Some well-defined problems are undecidable, so no algorithm can solve them for every input.

sections.heading: The halting problem
sections.text:
The halting problem asks whether a given program halts on a given input. Turing proved by contradiction that it is undecidable.

Suppose that a program H(P, x) always correctly decides whether P halts on x. Build a program D that takes a program P and asks H about P run on its own code. If H says “halts”, D loops forever. If H says “does not halt”, D stops at once.

Now run D on its own code. If D halts, H said that it does not halt. If D does not halt, H said that it halts. H is wrong in both cases, so H cannot exist.

sections.heading: P, NP and NP-completeness
sections.text:
P is the class of decision problems that can be solved in polynomial time. NP is the class of decision problems whose “yes” answers can be verified in polynomial time, given a suitable certificate. NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not “not polynomial”. Every problem in P is also in NP. Whether P = NP is the best-known open question in the field.

A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. It is NP-complete if it is also in NP. The Cook-Levin theorem showed that the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-complete. To prove that a new problem X is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem to X. Students often reverse this direction.

keyPoints: The halting problem is undecidable.
The Church-Turing thesis is not a formal theorem.
NP means that “yes” answers can be verified in polynomial time.
NP-complete means both in NP and NP-hard.
To show that X is hard, reduce a known hard problem to X.
Whether P = NP remains unknown.

en.title: Compilers and language translation
en.short: The phases of a compiler, from tokens and parse trees to intermediate code and optimisation.

sections.heading: The phases
sections.text: A compiler translates source code into a lower-level language, and it reports errors. The front end depends on the source language, and the back end depends on the target machine. An intermediate representation between them allows one front end to serve many back ends.

sections.heading: Lexical and syntax analysis
sections.text:
The lexical analyser, or scanner, groups characters into tokens. Regular expressions usually define tokens, and finite automata recognise them. The statement
total = price + rate * 2
becomes the tokens: identifier total, operator =, identifier price, operator +, identifier rate, operator *, number 2.

The parser checks the tokens against a context-free grammar and builds a tree. This grammar gives * a higher precedence than +:
E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → ( E ) | id | number

Because of this grammar, 2 + 3 * 4 groups as 2 + (3 * 4) and gives 14. Top-down parsers, such as LL parsers, start from the start symbol, and they cannot use left-recursive rules such as E → E + T without rewriting them. Bottom-up parsers, such as LR parsers, build from the tokens upward and can handle them.

sections.heading: Semantic analysis and intermediate code
sections.text:
Semantic analysis checks meaning. It uses a symbol table, which records each name’s type and scope. It reports errors that a grammar cannot detect, such as using an undeclared variable or adding a number to a Boolean value where the language forbids this.

The compiler then produces intermediate code. Three-address code has at most one operator on the right side of each instruction. The example statement becomes:
t1 = rate * 2
t2 = price + t1
total = t2

sections.heading: Optimisation and code generation
sections.text:
Optimisation improves the code without changing its meaning. Constant folding replaces 60 * 60 with 3600 at compile time. Dead code elimination removes code that can never affect the result.

Code generation selects machine instructions and allocates registers.

keyPoints: The main phases: lexical, syntax and semantic analysis, then intermediate code, optimisation and code generation.
Regular expressions define tokens; context-free grammars define syntax.
The symbol table records names, types and scopes.
Grammar rules can encode operator precedence.
Optimisation must preserve the program’s meaning.

en.title: Computer security
en.short: Security goals, cryptography, passwords, common attacks and laws on data protection.

sections.heading: Goals and principles
sections.text: Security aims for confidentiality, integrity and availability, which are called the CIA triad. Authentication checks who you are. Authorisation decides what you may do. A good principle is least privilege, which gives each user only the access needed.

sections.heading: Cryptography
sections.text:
Symmetric encryption uses one shared key, and it is fast. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key. It solves the problem of sharing keys, and it supports digital signatures, but it is slower. Systems such as TLS use asymmetric methods to agree on a key and then use symmetric encryption for the data.

Worked example: RSA with very small numbers.
Choose primes p = 5 and q = 11, so n = 55.
φ(n) = (5 − 1)(11 − 1) = 40.
Choose e = 3, which has no common factor with 40.
Find d = 27, because 3 × 27 = 81, and 81 mod 40 = 1.
Encrypt the message 7: 7³ mod 55 = 343 mod 55 = 13.
Decrypt: 13²⁷ mod 55 = 7.

Real keys are thousands of bits long, and real systems also add random padding.

A cryptographic hash gives a fixed-size digest and cannot practically be reversed.

sections.heading: Passwords and common attacks
sections.text:
Never store passwords as plain text. Store a salted hash from a deliberately slow password-hashing function. The salt is a random value for each user, and it defeats precomputed tables.

SQL injection occurs when user input becomes part of a query. Parameterised queries prevent it. Cross-site scripting (XSS) occurs when a site includes untrusted input in a page, so that a script runs in another user’s browser. Encode output to prevent it.

sections.heading: Law and ethics
sections.text: Rules differ by country. Examples include Nigeria’s Cybercrimes Act 2015 (amended in 2024) and Data Protection Act 2023, Ghana’s Data Protection Act 2012, Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019, South Africa’s POPIA, the EU’s GDPR and its UK version. Check the current official text. Test only systems for which you have written permission.

keyPoints: The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Symmetric encryption is fast; asymmetric encryption solves key sharing.
Authentication is about identity; authorisation is about permissions.
Store passwords as salted, slow hashes.
Parameterised queries prevent SQL injection.

en.title: Computing ethics and the profession
en.short: Ethical analysis, professional codes, responsibility for software, intellectual property and social impact.

sections.heading: Ethics, law and analysis
sections.text:
Ethics asks what we ought to do. Law states what is required or forbidden in one place at one time. Something legal may still be questioned on ethical grounds, and cultural context shapes how people judge a decision.

Consequentialist views judge an action by its results. Duty and rights views ask which obligations apply. Virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do. Ubuntu, from southern Africa, stresses people’s bonds with their community. No single framework settles every case.

sections.heading: Worked example: a stakeholder analysis
sections.text:
A clinic asks for an app that sends test results by text message. Many patients share phones.
Stakeholders: patients, families, clinic staff and the developer.
Benefit: results arrive sooner, with less travel.
Risk: a relative may read private health information.
Duties: confidentiality, consent and the local data law.
Options: send the result, send only “your result is ready” with a code, or let each patient choose.

People may weigh these points differently. The aim is a decision that you can justify.

sections.heading: Professional responsibility
sections.text:
Bodies such as ACM and IEEE publish codes of conduct. The ACM code treats the public good as the primary consideration. In Nigeria, CPN regulates the profession by statute.

Professionals are responsible for competent work, honest estimates and reporting risks. Between 1985 and 1987, the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine gave patients massive overdoses, and some died. Race conditions in its software contributed, and hardware interlocks from earlier models had been removed.

sections.heading: Rights and social impact
sections.text:
Copyright, patents, trade secrets and software licences protect intellectual property. Their rules differ by country. These notes are not legal advice, so check the current official source.

Other common topics are privacy, biased automated decisions, accessibility, fairness and health at work, and the energy use and waste of computing. Some questions remain contested, such as how to balance surveillance with privacy, how to moderate online content and how automation will affect jobs. Learn the main arguments on each side, and separate evidence from values.

keyPoints: Legal and ethical are not the same thing, and both depend on context.
No single ethical framework settles every case.
Stakeholder analysis lists who is affected, the benefits, the risks and the options.
Professional codes guide judgement, but they do not replace it.
Software failures can cause serious harm, so reliability is an ethical matter.
Laws on data and intellectual property differ by country.

en.title: Web and mobile systems
en.short: How web applications are structured, HTTP and APIs, performance, and building for mobile devices.

sections.heading: Structure of a web application
sections.text: A web application follows the client-server model. In the browser, HTML gives the structure of a page, CSS gives its appearance and JavaScript gives its behaviour. The front end is the part that runs there. The back end runs on servers. It holds the business rules, checks data and talks to a database. Never rely on checks in the browser alone, because a user can change or bypass them.

sections.heading: HTTP and APIs
sections.text:
An API is a defined way for programs to communicate. Many web APIs follow the REST style, in which resources have addresses and standard HTTP methods act on them.
GET reads a resource.
POST usually creates one.
PUT replaces one.
DELETE removes one.

Status codes group the results: 2xx means success (200 OK), 3xx redirection, 4xx a client error (404 Not Found) and 5xx a server error (500).

HTTP is stateless, so applications use cookies or tokens to remember a signed-in user.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: Many users have slow or expensive connections. A page of 2 MB on a 1 Mbit/s link takes at least (2 × 8) ÷ 1 = 16 seconds to transfer.

sections.heading: Mobile systems
sections.text:
There are three common approaches. Native apps are written for one platform, and they get the best access to its features. Cross-platform frameworks share most code between platforms. Web apps run in the browser and need no installation, but they have more limited access to the device.

Mobile development has special constraints. The system may pause or close an app at any moment, so an app must save its state. This behaviour is known as the app life cycle. Apps must ask for permission to use the camera, location and similar features, and they should request only what they need.

Offline-first design stores data on the device and synchronises it when a connection returns. The design must decide what happens when two devices change the same record.

keyPoints: HTML gives structure, CSS appearance and JavaScript behaviour.
Always validate data on the server.
Status code groups: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
Offline-first design needs a plan for conflicting changes.
Mobile apps must save state, because the system can close them at any moment.

en.title: Human-computer interaction
en.short: User-centred design, usability principles, evaluation methods, accessibility and Fitts’ law.

sections.heading: What HCI studies
sections.text: Human-computer interaction (HCI) studies how people use technology and how to design it so that it serves them. Usability is commonly described through effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction: can people complete their task, how much effort does it take, and how do they feel about the experience? A system can work correctly and still fail because people cannot use it.

sections.heading: User-centred design
sections.text:
User-centred design is an iterative process:
1. Understand users, their tasks and their context through interviews and observation.
2. Specify their needs.
3. Produce designs, starting with low-fidelity prototypes such as paper sketches.
4. Evaluate them with users, and repeat.

Consider the real context of use. A health worker using a shared phone outdoors, with poor network coverage, has different needs from an office worker with a large screen.

sections.heading: Principles and evaluation
sections.text:
Well-known guidelines include Nielsen’s usability heuristics. They ask for visible system status, consistency, error prevention, clear ways to undo actions and helpful error messages.

Heuristic evaluation lets a few experts inspect an interface against such guidelines. It is quick, but it does not involve real users. In usability testing, representative users attempt realistic tasks while researchers record success, time and errors.

sections.heading: Accessibility and Fitts’ law
sections.text:
Accessible design includes people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive impairments. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the main international reference. For example, level AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Provide text alternatives for images, and allow keyboard use.

Fitts’ law predicts the time to point at a target. One common form is T = a + b log₂(D/W + 1), where D is the distance and W the target’s width. Worked example: with a = 0.1 s, b = 0.15 s, D = 300 and W = 20, we get log₂(16) = 4 and T = 0.1 + 0.15 × 4 = 0.7 s. Large, near targets are faster to reach, so this matters for touch buttons.

keyPoints: Usability covers effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction.
User-centred design repeats research, design and evaluation.
Heuristic evaluation uses experts; usability testing uses real users.
WCAG level AA asks for 4.5:1 contrast on normal text.
Fitts’ law: larger, nearer targets are faster to reach.

en.title: Artificial intelligence: agents, search and knowledge representation
en.short: Intelligent agents, heuristic search, knowledge representation and how they relate to machine learning.

sections.heading: What AI studies
sections.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) builds systems for tasks that seem to need intelligence. An agent perceives its environment and acts on it. A rational agent chooses the action expected to give the best result.

Turing’s 1950 test asks whether a judge can tell a machine from a person in conversation. Searle’s 1980 Chinese Room argues that following rules is not understanding, and this conclusion is disputed. Narrow AI handles particular tasks. Whether general AI could match people across most tasks is also debated.

sections.heading: Search and heuristics
sections.text:
Many problems are searches through states. The number of states often grows very fast, which is called combinatorial explosion.

A heuristic estimates the remaining cost. A* search expands the state with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g is the cost so far and h is the estimate. If h never overestimates, A* finds a cheapest path. Search methods trade off completeness, optimality, time and memory.

Worked example: S→A 2, S→B 4, A→G 6, B→G 3, with h(A) = 6 and h(B) = 2.
f(A) = 2 + 6 = 8 and f(B) = 4 + 2 = 6, so expand B.
G is reached through B with f = 7 + 0 = 7, which is below 8.
The best path is S, B, G, with cost 7.

sections.heading: Knowledge representation
sections.text:
Predicate logic states rules exactly.
Rule: ∀x (Student(x) → HasID(x))
Clause form: ¬Student(x) ∨ HasID(x)
Fact: Student(Kofi)
Resolution combines the two clauses and gives HasID(Kofi).
