A semantic network draws concepts as nodes and relationships as links. A frame groups a concept’s attributes into slots. An expert system combines a knowledge base with an inference engine.

sections.heading: Links with machine learning
sections.text: Machine learning is a branch of AI. Symbolic systems use knowledge that people write down, so their reasoning is often easy to inspect. Learned models take patterns from data, and they can be harder to explain. Natural language processing and image recognition now rely heavily on learning.

keyPoints: An agent perceives its environment and acts on it.
The Turing test and the Chinese Room are about behaviour and understanding, and both are debated.
A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n), and it finds a cheapest path if h never overestimates.
Combinatorial explosion is why heuristics matter.
Logic, semantic networks and frames are ways to represent knowledge.
Machine learning is one branch of AI, not the whole field.

en.title: Machine learning
en.short: Learning from data: types of learning, gradient descent, overfitting, evaluation and fairness.

sections.heading: Types of learning
sections.text: Machine learning builds models from data rather than from fixed rules. In supervised learning, the data include the correct outputs, and the task is classification or regression. In unsupervised learning, there are no labels, and the task may be clustering or dimensionality reduction. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by acting and receiving rewards.

sections.heading: Training by gradient descent
sections.text:
Training usually means minimising a loss function, which measures the model’s error. Gradient descent moves each parameter a small step against the gradient. The learning rate sets the step size.

Worked example: fit y = wx to the points (1, 2) and (2, 4), using mean squared error, L = (1/n) Σ (wx − y)². The gradient is dL/dw = (2/n) Σ x(wx − y). Start with w = 0 and a learning rate of 0.1.
Step 1: gradient = (2/2) × [1(0 − 2) + 2(0 − 4)] = −10, so w = 0 − 0.1 × (−10) = 1.

The value of w moves towards the correct answer, 2.

Neural networks stack layers of linear functions with non-linear activation functions. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute gradients efficiently.

sections.heading: Generalisation
sections.text:
The aim is good performance on new data. A model that overfits learns noise in its training data, so it does well there and badly on new data.

Split the data into training, validation and test sets. Use the test set only at the end. k-fold cross-validation gives a stronger estimate on small datasets.

sections.heading: Evaluation and responsibility
sections.text:
Accuracy can mislead when classes are unequal. If 99% of transactions are genuine, a model that always says “genuine” has 99% accuracy and detects no fraud.

Worked example: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20 and TN = 130.
Accuracy = 170/200 = 0.85
Precision = 40/50 = 0.80
Recall = 40/60 ≈ 0.67

Models can repeat bias in their training data, and they may perform worse for groups that are poorly represented. Test performance across groups.

keyPoints: Supervised learning uses labels; unsupervised learning does not.
Gradient descent moves parameters against the gradient.
Overfitting means good training results and poor results on new data.
Keep the test set separate until the end.
Use precision and recall when classes are unbalanced.

en.title: Distributed systems
en.short: Partial failure, time and ordering, replication, consistency, consensus and the CAP theorem.

sections.heading: Why distribution is hard
sections.text: A distributed system is a set of computers that cooperate through messages. It also brings partial failure: one part can fail while the others continue. If a reply does not arrive, the sender cannot tell whether the message was lost, the reply was lost, or the other machine is merely slow.

sections.heading: Time and ordering
sections.text:
Physical clocks drift, so they cannot safely order events across machines. Lamport’s logical clocks use the happens-before relation. Each process increases a counter for each event. Each message carries the counter, and the receiver sets its own counter to max(local, received) + 1.

Worked example: a process with clock 2 receives a message stamped 4. Its clock becomes max(2, 4) + 1 = 5.

If event a happens before event b, then C(a) < C(b). The reverse is not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Replication and consistency
sections.text:
Replication keeps copies of data for availability and speed, but then the copies must be kept in agreement. Strong models, such as linearisability, make the system appear to have one copy. Eventual consistency only promises that replicas will agree if updates stop.

Quorums are one method. With N copies, a write waits for W replies and a read waits for R replies. If W + R > N, each read overlaps with the latest completed write. With N = 5, W = 3 and R = 3, the sum 6 is greater than 5, so they overlap.

The CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a system must give up either strong consistency or availability.

sections.heading: Consensus and transactions
sections.text:
Consensus lets nodes agree on one value, even when some of them fail. Paxos and Raft are the best-known algorithms for crash failures. They need a majority, so 5 nodes tolerate 2 crashes.

Two-phase commit coordinates a transaction across machines. The coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then tells them to commit or abort. If the coordinator fails at the wrong moment, participants can block.

keyPoints: Partial failure is the central difficulty of distributed systems.
Lamport clocks order events consistently but cannot prove concurrency.
W + R > N makes read and write quorums overlap.
CAP is about the choice during a network partition.
Raft and Paxos need a majority of nodes to work.

en.title: Research methods in computing
en.short: Planning computing research: questions, methods, experiments, statistics, ethics and writing up.

sections.heading: From topic to question
sections.text:
Begin with a focused question. “How can AI help schools?” is too broad. “Does automatic feedback improve first-year students’ marks in programming assignments?” can be tested.

A literature review shows what is already known and where the gap lies.

sections.heading: Choosing a method
sections.text:
The question decides the method. Experiments test cause and effect by changing one factor and controlling others. Benchmarks compare the performance of systems. Surveys gather views from many people. Interviews and case studies give depth. Design science builds an artefact and evaluates it.

A good study also considers threats to validity. Internal validity asks whether the treatment really caused the effect. External validity asks whether the results apply elsewhere. Construct validity asks whether you measured what you intended.

sections.heading: Experiments and statistics
sections.text:
Performance measurements vary, so repeat each run and report the spread as well as the mean. State the hardware, software versions and settings. Share data and code when you can, so that others can reproduce your results.

Worked example: 25 runs of a query have a mean of 120 ms and a standard deviation of 10 ms. A 95% confidence interval uses t ≈ 2.06:
120 ± 2.06 × 10 ÷ √25 = 120 ± 4.1
So the interval is about 115.9 to 124.1 ms.

A p-value is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. Statistical significance also does not mean that an effect is large or important, so report the effect size.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text:
Research with people normally needs approval from an ethics committee, as well as informed consent and protection of personal data. Rules depend on the institution and the country. Cite all sources, and never present another person’s work as your own.

A typical dissertation has an introduction, a literature review, methods, results, a discussion and a conclusion. Report negative results and limitations honestly.

keyPoints: A good research question is focused and can be tested.
The question decides the method, not the reverse.
Consider internal, external and construct validity.
A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Report variation and enough detail for others to reproduce your work.
